title: Against the Mountains of Israel
summary: Ezekiel is told to turn and prophesy against the mountains of Israel, where the people had built high places, altars, and idols. God will destroy those shrines and leave the bodies of the worshipers lying before their idols. Yet a remnant will survive among the nations, remember how they grieved God, and loathe themselves for what they did, and in all of it they will know that he is the LORD.
story: Chapters 4 and 5 focused on Jerusalem and its coming siege. Chapter 6 widens the lens to the whole land. The mountains and hills of Israel had been the sites of the worship that the prophets had condemned for centuries: local shrines where the LORD was worshiped alongside other gods, or confused with them. Ezekiel now declares that judgment will reach every one of those places. The chapter also gives the first clear statement in the book that survivors will come to repentance in exile (verses 8 to 10). Ezekiel will later address the same mountains again, in chapter 36, with the opposite message: they will be replanted, repopulated, and blessed. Chapter 6 is the dark half of that pair.
historical:
The oracle belongs to the same years as the surrounding chapters, between Ezekiel's call in 593 BC and the fall of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC, while Zedekiah ruled Judah as a vassal of Babylon. The worship it condemns had deep roots. The books of Kings measure nearly every ruler of Israel and Judah by whether he removed the high places. King Hezekiah, in the late eighth century BC, and King Josiah, in the late seventh century, both carried out reforms that tore down shrines and centralized worship in Jerusalem (2 Kings 18:4; 23:4-20). Josiah died in 609 BC, and the prophets indicate that his reforms did not last. By Ezekiel's day the local shrines were active again.

The closing phrase, “from the wilderness to Diblah” (verse 14), is meant to cover the whole land. No place named Diblah is otherwise known, and many scholars think it is an early copying slip for Riblah, a town in Syria on the northern edge of Israel's traditional territory, since the Hebrew letters d and r look very similar. Riblah was where Nebuchadnezzar later judged Zedekiah (2 Kings 25:6-7).
cultural:
A high place was an outdoor or hilltop shrine with an altar, sometimes a standing stone or wooden pole, and sometimes a small building. In the ancient world, hills and green trees were thought to be places where the divine was near and where fertility could be secured. Canaanite religion honored gods such as Baal, the storm god who brought rain, and goddesses associated with fertility, and Israelites often folded these practices into their worship of the LORD. Verse 13 gathers the typical settings: every high hill, the mountaintops, and “under every green tree and leafy oak,” a stock phrase in Deuteronomy, Kings, Jeremiah, and Hosea for this kind of worship.

Leaving unburied bodies beside altars was the most complete way to defile a shrine. For an Israelite, contact with a corpse made a person or place ritually unclean (Numbers 19:11-16), and King Josiah had used human bones to desecrate the altar at Bethel (2 Kings 23:16). The image in verses 4 and 5 therefore says two things at once: the worshipers die, and their holy places become unclean forever.
literary: The chapter is a single oracle addressed to the land itself, a technique prophets used to make the whole of Israel's territory a witness (compare Micah 6:1-2). It opens with the formula that begins many of Ezekiel's messages, “the word of the LORD came to me,” and the command to “set your face against” the addressee, a gesture of confrontation Ezekiel uses repeatedly. The oracle falls into three movements: destruction of the shrines (verses 3 to 7), a remnant who remember (verses 8 to 10), and a lament followed by more judgment (verses 11 to 14). Each movement ends with some form of the recognition formula, “you will know that I am the LORD,” which occurs four times in fourteen verses and becomes the signature of the whole book.

outline.t: The prophet sets his face against the mountains
High places, altars, and idols destroyed
A remnant among the nations remembers and loathes its sin
Clap, stomp, and cry out: sword, famine, and plague
Bodies among the idols and the land made desolate

doctrines.note: The chapter treats idolatry not as a harmless variety of worship but as unfaithfulness to the God who had bound himself to Israel. Verse 9 describes it in relational terms: God was grieved by their “adulterous hearts” and by eyes that lusted after idols.

Repentance in verses 8 to 10 begins with remembering: the survivors will remember God, see how they grieved him, and loathe what they did. Ezekiel's picture of repentance is not a bargain for better treatment but a changed view of oneself before God.

The repeated phrase “you will know that I am the LORD” shows that God's acts in history, both judgment and later rescue, are a form of self-revelation. The goal is not merely that Israel be punished but that it come to know who God truly is.

words.note: Gillulim, idols. This is Ezekiel's favorite word for idols, and most of its uses in the Old Testament are in his book. Its origin is uncertain; many scholars connect it with a root meaning to roll, and suggest it was a contemptuous word, something like dung pellets or lumps. Whatever its roots, Ezekiel uses it with open scorn.

Bamah, high place. The word can mean a height or ridge, but in the historical books and the prophets it usually refers to a local shrine. Its repeated condemnation reflects the Deuteronomic demand that sacrificial worship be offered at the one place God would choose (Deuteronomy 12), and the danger that local shrines absorbed Canaanite practice.

Zanah, to be unfaithful or to prostitute oneself. In verse 9 it describes Israel's heart turning away from God. The prophets regularly use sexual unfaithfulness as a picture of idolatry because the covenant was understood as an exclusive bond, like marriage. Ezekiel develops the image at great length in chapters 16 and 23.

Yada, to know. The phrase built on it, “you will know that I am the LORD,” occurs more than sixty times in Ezekiel. The knowing is more than information; it is recognition, often forced by events, of who God is and what he has done.

christ: The link to Christ here is thematic. Ezekiel pictures a remnant who, scattered among the nations, finally remember their God and turn from idols. The New Testament describes the gospel reaching exactly that kind of people: Paul says the believers in Thessalonica turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God (1 Thessalonians 1:9). Jesus also told a Samaritan woman that the time was coming when true worship would not be tied to a particular mountain but offered in spirit and truth (John 4:21-24). The hilltop shrines Ezekiel condemns represent worship shaped by human desire and anxiety. In Christ the question of where God is to be found receives its final answer: in the person of the Son.

hard.q: Why would God want survivors to loathe themselves? Isn't that psychologically harmful?
hard.a: The phrase in verse 9 can sound like a call to self-hatred, and some readers have been hurt by teaching that pressed it that way. The Hebrew describes a strong revulsion at one's own actions, the kind of disgust a person feels on finally seeing clearly what they have done. In context it is paired with remembering God and knowing him (verses 9 and 10), and elsewhere Ezekiel links the same response to God's forgiveness and new heart (20:43; 36:31). The point is not that people are worthless but that sin, seen honestly, is ugly. Christian tradition has distinguished between this kind of godly sorrow, which leads to life, and a despairing shame that leads away from God (2 Corinthians 7:10). If shame about your past feels crushing rather than freeing, it is worth talking with a pastor or a counselor you trust.

questions: The people worshiped the LORD and the local gods side by side. What does divided worship look like in a modern life?
Verse 9 says God was grieved by his people's unfaithful hearts. How does it change your picture of sin to think of it as grieving someone rather than breaking a rule?
The remnant's repentance starts with remembering. What would it mean for you to remember God honestly in a hard season?
